# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Clinical Review

### Introduction
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has revolutionized the management of severe symptomatic aortic stenosis, becoming the standard of care for many patients across the risk spectrum [1]. While transfemoral (TF) access remains the preferred route due to its lower complication rates and faster recovery, severe peripheral artery disease (PAD), extensive calcification, extreme tortuosity, and small vessel caliber preclude its use in up to 10% of candidates [2]. Historically, patients ineligible for TF access were managed via alternative surgical access pathways, including transapical (TA), transaortic (TAo), or subclavian/axillary approaches [3]. However, surgical transthoracic approaches (TA and TAo) are associated with elevated risks of bleeding, pleural complications, prolonged hospitalization, and higher rates of acute kidney injury (AKI) [4, 5]. In search of a less invasive percutaneous alternative, transcaval (cavo-aortic) access was developed [6]. This novel technique utilizes the abdominal venous system as a conduit to introduce large-bore sheaths into the arterial system, successfully bypassing hostile iliofemoral vessels [7, 8].

### Anatomy and Pre-Procedural Evaluation
The success of transcaval access relies heavily on the close anatomical relationship between the abdominal aorta and the inferior vena cava (IVC) below the level of the renal arteries [9]. High-resolution computed tomography (CT) angiography is indispensable during the pre-procedural planning phase [10]. Crucial steps in CT planning include identifying an optimal crossing window where the IVC and aorta are in close contact, typically free of intervening structures like bowel loops, major retroperitoneal veins, or primary lumbar arteries [11]. Additionally, operators must evaluate the target aortic wall for the absence of severe circumferential calcification, thick eccentric atheroma, or aneurysmal disease, which could compromise crossing or safe closure [12].

### Procedural Technique and Closure
Standardized techniques have been developed to ensure safety and reproducibility [13, 14]. The procedure begins with bilateral femoral access: venous access for the delivery system in the IVC and arterial access for a target snare or catheter in the abdominal aorta [15]. Using fluoroscopic and angiographic guidance, a dedicated crossing system consisting of a guidewire energized by electrosurgery is advanced from the IVC to puncture the aortic wall [16]. Once the wire enters the aorta, it is snared or advanced into the thoracic aorta, facilitating the exchange for a rigid, supportive guidewire [17]. A large-bore sheath can then be safely advanced across the aortocaval tract to perform the structural intervention [18, 19].

Following the completion of the main structural procedure, the transcaval tract is closed to prevent catastrophic retroperitoneal hemorrhage [20]. This is typically achieved by deploying a nitinol vascular occluder, most commonly the Amplatzer Duct Occluder (ADO) I or II, across the aortocaval crossing site [21]. The inherent pressure gradient between the aorta and the IVC ensures that any residual leak flow is directed into the low-pressure venous system rather than the retroperitoneum, resulting in a hemodynamically insignificant aortocaval fistula that frequently closes spontaneously within several months [22].

### Clinical Outcomes and Comparative Evidence
Pivotal data from prospective registries, notably the National Institutes of Health (NIH) transcaval registry, have demonstrated high technical success rates exceeding 98% [23]. Despite the seemingly aggressive nature of traversing the retroperitoneum, the rate of major vascular complications is remarkably low when performed by experienced operators [24]. Clinical comparative trials have highlighted that transcaval access is associated with significantly lower rates of post-procedural AKI and shorter hospital stays compared to traditional surgical transthoracic alternative accesses [25, 26]. In propensity-matched cohorts, patients undergoing transcaval TAVR exhibited superior 30-day survival and fewer adverse events than those undergoing transapical or transaortic TAVR [27]. Meta-analyses of contemporary registry data have further validated these findings, reinforcing transcaval access as a first-line alternative when transfemoral access is anatomically hostile [28].

### Complications and Future Directions
The primary complications associated with transcaval access include retroperitoneal hematoma, major vascular injury requiring covered stents, and device embolization [29]. Although the learning curve is steep, standardization of the technique and improved pre-procedural CT planning have dramatically reduced the incidence of these events [30]. Today, the utility of transcaval access extends beyond TAVR to other large-bore structural and endovascular interventions, including thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) and the insertion of mechanical circulatory support devices like the Impella [23].
